codeVsHuman.method: Code built and tests passing is the share of the Built and Automated tests checks that passed. The separate Device and real-world checks recorded figure is the share of Real device, Real-world check and Ready to call Available that passed. It includes AI tests on real devices; it does not mean a person checked every feature. The final Ready check needs a human look, recorded by Nick. These separate figures keep their existing checklist method. Group figures are the average of their features and are never rounded up to 100. A feature shows "Code 100%" only when both of those code checks passed and no CODE item is still open; it counts as "Confirmed working on real devices" only when all five checks passed. Remaining counts are open road-to-100 items. All 70 features are counted, including those that are planned or on hold.

fullProgress.method: Each area is the average of its feature rows in this file (listed by name in rowNames). Code checklist is the share of the Built and Automated tests checks that passed. Device and real-world checks recorded is the share of the Real device, Real-world check and Ready to call Available checks that passed. confirmedOnRealDevices counts rows with all five checks passed and no open code item. The same method is used on release-evidence.html. A percentage is evidence coverage, not a promise that every device, route or situation works.

howToRead: Each feature has five checks. Built is worth 24 points. Passing automated tests adds 25. Running on a real phone or PC adds 25. The real-world check adds 25. A dated realistic check can be performed by an AI tester on real devices, or by a person, when its evidence covers the feature’s actual use. A QA server or test fixture does not by itself disqualify that check. Muted or state-only evidence cannot prove sound, timing or another behavior it did not judge. Relevant open failures and stated record limits stay in force. Realistic, dated AI checks on real devices count toward the Real-world check, and so toward 99%. Only Nick records Ready (100%), after he and Claude confirm the feature together with no errors found. Any open failure caps a feature at 90% until it is fixed. At 99%, all four checks have passed and no known error is open. That means tested and confirmed working within the recorded checks. The last 1% is a human look, not more building. Nick looks with his own eyes, he and Claude confirm the feature together with no errors found, and only then does Nick record Ready. An open known error caps the score at 90%. Existing record limits can keep it lower. At 99%, the label is "Tested and working, waiting for a human look". At 100%, it is "Ready, a human confirmed". Each row says what was proven, when it was tested and what remains unverified. Each feature also has a road-to-100 list: what 100% means, what is done, and what remains, grouped as CODE (we can build or fix it), DEVICE (needs a real phone, PC, TV or car), NICK (his decision, account, money or legal) and BLOCKED.

features.leftToReach100: Update Oct 27, 2026: fixes for both open problems below were merged into the main code on Oct 27, 2026 (Snakes and Ladders now ends the game when a move reaches square 100, including by a ladder, and the winner’s name is kept after the host leaves a finished room). They were independently reviewed and the PC test suites ran, but nobody has retried them on an installed build with two real phones, so both issues stay open and the score stays 90%. Open known issues (cap this row at 90%): 2, both found on Oct 26, 2026 on tester51 (reported by about 4:48 PM Eastern). (1) Snakes and Ladders: “Host rolled 5 and climbed 80 to 100” did not end the game at once: the side label read “home” yet the guest kept rolling (6, 6, 2) and the win came only at the host’s next roll about a minute later; landing on square 100, including by a ladder, should win immediately. (2) After the host leaves a FINISHED room, the guest still in the room sees “Player wins!” and “Player = 1” instead of “Host wins!” and “Host = 1”; in Snakes and Ladders the guest showed “0” next to the guest’s name and the host’s score of 1 vanished. A fix (ordinary code with new rule tests) was merged on Oct 27, 2026 and awaits a retest on an installed build; once retested the row returns to 99%. Two smaller findings, not counted: finished or empty rooms stay listed (“1 in this game”, “Waiting for a player” behind a finished round), and the host showed “2 guests connected” after opening the game room (probably counting its own web view or a stale connection). The Real-world check is ticked from this realistic two-phone run: a native Galaxy S9+ host and a separate Pixel 3 guest in Chrome on the same home Wi-Fi (no hotspot; the guest joined by typing the join address shown on the host; the list showed 42 guest games). Played to a natural end with both screens showing the same final state each time: Drop Four (13 moves, host won with a vertical four; an out-of-turn tap and a tap on a full column were ignored), Snakes and Ladders (about 25 rolls each, host won; a disabled Roll tapped out of turn was ignored), Mancala (a 24 to 24 draw; an out-of-turn tap ignored) and Dots and Boxes 3x3 (24 lines, the guest won 6 boxes to 3). Rejoin passed (Mancala, mid-game 14 to 13): the guest’s tab was closed and reopened at the same address and kept the same name, seat and state. Host stop passed: the guest showed “Slow connection. Still trying...” and about 12 seconds later “The host has stopped Campsite, or their phone is asleep or off Wi-Fi...” with the finished board still visible, and the host returned cleanly to the Campsite start screen. Limits: Checkers, Sea Battle, Chess, Nine Men’s Morris, Crazy Eights as a guest game, card, party and poll games, three or more players, bots, tournaments, hotspot and Wi-Fi Direct routes, cellular guests, sound, an illegal move in Dots and Boxes, a rejoin in a finished game and long unattended runs were not tested; the phones were muted. checkDefinitions.Built: The code exists and works in the build.
checkDefinitions.Automated tests: The test suite for it passes.
checkDefinitions.Real device: We ran it on a real phone, PC or TV and it worked.
checkDefinitions.Real-world check: A dated realistic check can be performed by an AI tester on real devices, or by a person, when its evidence covers the feature’s actual use. A QA server or test fixture does not by itself disqualify that check. Muted or state-only evidence cannot prove sound, timing or another behavior it did not judge. Relevant open failures and stated record limits stay in force. Realistic, dated AI checks on real devices count toward the Real-world check, and so toward 99%. Only Nick records Ready (100%), after he and Claude confirm the feature together with no errors found. Any open failure caps a feature at 90% until it is fixed. Historical checks remain dated evidence, not certification of a newer build.
checkDefinitions.Ready to call Available: Nick has looked with his own eyes, and he and Claude have confirmed the feature together with no errors found. Only Nick records this check. It is worth the last 1 point: a human look, not more building.

scoring.waitingLabel: Tested and working, waiting for a human look

tiers.label: Purple: Tested and working, waiting for a human look
Green: proven checks, open issue or record limit

scoring.rule: percentComplete is worked out from features[].checks and features[].openIssues by site-data/progress-score.js: Built 24, Automated tests 25, Real device 25, Real-world check 25, Ready to call Available 1 (only Nick records it). The first four add up to 99. A feature reaches 99 only when all four are true and openIssues is 0 (omitted means 0). An open known error caps the score at 90. An optional percentCap, explained by scoreNote, is a further limit. Check with: node site-data/check-progress-score.js.
scoring.explanation: Each feature has five checks. Built is worth 24 points. Passing automated tests adds 25. Running on a real phone or PC adds 25. The real-world check adds 25. A dated realistic check can be performed by an AI tester on real devices, or by a person, when its evidence covers the feature’s actual use. A QA server or test fixture does not by itself disqualify that check. Muted or state-only evidence cannot prove sound, timing or another behavior it did not judge. Relevant open failures and stated record limits stay in force. Realistic, dated AI checks on real devices count toward the Real-world check, and so toward 99%. Only Nick records Ready (100%), after he and Claude confirm the feature together with no errors found. Any open failure caps a feature at 90% until it is fixed. At 99%, all four checks have passed and no known error is open. That means tested and confirmed working within the recorded checks. The last 1% is a human look, not more building. Nick looks with his own eyes, he and Claude confirm the feature together with no errors found, and only then does Nick record Ready. An open known error caps the score at 90%. Existing record limits can keep it lower. At 99%, the label is "Tested and working, waiting for a human look". At 100%, it is "Ready, a human confirmed". Each row says what was proven, when it was tested and what remains unverified.
